title: Prepositions that stick to the tail
goal: Say where things and rooms are with six place endings, tell *van* apart from *nincs*, and spot the group of words that does **not** stick on.
bekal: answer *hol*, *hová* and *honnan* with the right ending
say what exists and what doesn't with *van*, *vannak*, *nincs*, *nincsenek*
use *mellett*, *alatt*, *előtt* and friends as separate words

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Az új lakásban
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a small apartment in the seventh district. Anna comes over to have a look.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Szia! Milyen szép lakás! Hol van a konyha?
lines.id: Hi! What a nice apartment! Where is the kitchen?
lines.literal: hello! how nice apartment! where is the kitchen?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A konyha itt van, balra. A szoba pedig jobbra.
lines.id: The kitchen is here, on the left. And the room is on the right.
lines.literal: the kitchen here is, left-to. the room whereas right-to.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A könyvek a polcon vannak, az ablak mellett.
lines.id: The books are on the shelf, next to the window.
lines.literal: the book-PL the shelf-on they-are, the window next-to.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Igen, van. A fürdőszoba a konyha mellett van.
lines.id: Yes, there is. The bathroom is next to the kitchen.
lines.literal: yes, is. the bathroom the kitchen next-to is.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: And a balcony? Is there a balcony?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sajnos nincs erkély. De van egy nagy ablak.
lines.id: Unfortunately there is no balcony. But there is a big window.
lines.literal: unfortunately there-isn't balcony. but is a big window.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Is the apartment on the ground floor?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nem, a harmadik emeleten. Lift is van a házban.
lines.id: No, on the third floor. There is an elevator in the building too.
lines.literal: no, the third floor-on. elevator also is the house-in.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nagyon jó hely! És a bolt közel van?
lines.id: Great place! And is the shop close?
lines.literal: very good place! and the shop close is?

notes: **A polcon, but a szobában.** A shelf is a **surface** — things sit on top of it — so it takes *-on*. A room is an **enclosed space** — you are inside it — so it takes *-ban*. This split makes sense nine times out of ten, and that is enough for A1.

**Mellett does not stick on.** Look at *az ablak mellett* — written separately, with no ending on *ablak*. Hungarian has two tools for place: **endings** that attach, and **postpositions** (*névutó*) that stand alone. Both come **after** the noun, like English prepositions flipped around; the only difference is whether they fuse with it or not.
**Nincs, not nem van.** Hungarian has special words for "there isn't": *nincs* (singular) and *nincsenek* (plural). Building *nem van* sounds instantly odd — like saying "is-not is" in English.

**Van erkély? with no article.** When you ask whether something **exists** in general, the noun stays bare: *Van erkély?* (Is there a balcony?). The article shows up as soon as the noun is specific: *Hol van az erkély?* (Where is the balcony?).

**Is goes right after the word you stress.** *Fürdőszoba is van* = "there is a bathroom too". *Van is fürdőszoba* means something else. Put *is* directly **after** the word you mean — a small habit that marks a careful speaker.

**Balra, jobbra take the ending -ra.** Literally "to the left", "to the right" — direction, not location. The form for "on the left side" is *bal oldalon*. For everyday use, *balra* and *jobbra* cover almost every need.

grammars.title: Six place endings, two groups
body: All these endings answer one of three questions: *hol* (where), *hová* (where to), *honnan* (where from). What decides the group is whether the noun is thought of as a space or a surface.
after: Notice the sound pattern once more: the space group always contains a **b**, the surface group an **r** or **n**. These six endings are really just two patterns times three directions.

**The ending -on has three forms**, not two: *-on* (back vowels), *-en* (front vowels), *-ön* (rounded front vowels). *az asztalon*, *a széken*, *a földön*. Also, words ending in a vowel take just *-n*: *az ajtón*, *a kanapén*.

If you are unsure between space and surface for an odd noun — a party, a mountain, a meeting — use common sense first, then memorize the ones that miss. Even Hungarians can't explain why they say *a piacon* (at the market) but *a boltban* (in the shop).

grammars.title: Van, vannak, nincs, nincsenek
body: Four words that handle all of existence and non-existence.

head: Form
Say it
Used for
Example
rows: *Van egy ablak.* = There is a window.

after: Recall the rule from Unit 1: when a sentence says **who or what** something is, *van* is forbidden (*Ő tanár*). When it says **where something is or that it exists**, *van* is required (*A tanár az iskolában van*).
The negative follows the same rule: *Ő nem tanár* (He is not a teacher) uses *nem*, while *Nincs itt* (He isn't here) uses *nincs*.

grammars.title: Névutó — postpositions that don't stick on
body: This small group works like English prepositions, except that it stands after the noun. It never fuses with it, and the noun stays bare.

head: Magyar
Say it
English
Example
rows: *az ablak mellett* = next to the window
*a kép a kanapé fölött* = the picture above the sofa
*a ház előtt* = in front of the house
*az ablak és az ajtó között* = between the window and the door

after: *Fölött* versus *-on*: *a kép a falon van* (the picture is attached to the wall), *a lámpa az asztal fölött van* (the lamp hangs over the table without touching it). English uses "above" or "on" loosely for both; Hungarian separates touching from not touching.

This group also has "to" and "from" forms: *mellé* (to the side of), *mellől* (from beside), *alá* / *alól*, *elé* / *elől*, *mögé* / *mögül*. For A1, just recognize the "at" forms; the rest comes by itself through use.

sections.title: The home and what's in it

blocks.text: Use the habit suggested on the first pages: say each new word in this table right away with one ending. *szoba* → *szobában*, *polc* → *polcon*, *erkély* → *erkélyen*. Ten seconds per word, and vowel harmony stops being theory.

blocks.title: One small trap that often trips learners
items: *Hol vannak a könyvek?* uses the plural form because the thing is plural. English also marks this (*is* vs *are*), but Hungarian does it with *vannak* and *nincsenek* — so train yourself to check: plural things demand *vannak* and *nincsenek*, not *van* and *nincs*.
On the other hand, after a number the noun stays singular — and the verb goes singular with it: *Két könyv van az asztalon.* Not *vannak*.
